name: Ṛṣabha (Ṛṣabhanātha, Ādinātha)
summary: The first Tīrthaṅkara of this era, emblem the bull, son of the last patriarch (kulakara) Nābhi and Marudevī, born at Ayodhyā (Vinītā). As first king he taught humanity the arts of livelihood — arms, writing, agriculture, learning, trade and crafts — writing (the Brāhmī script) to his daughter Brāhmī and arithmetic to Sundarī, then renounced, fasted for about a year until Prince Śreyāṃsa offered him sugarcane juice (remembered on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā), attained omniscience and taught the dharma; he reached nirvāṇa on Mount Aṣṭāpada. His sons were the world-emperor Bharata and Bāhubali. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa also knows him as a renouncer-avatāra.

tradition.text: lived in the third age (suṣamā-duḥṣamā) of this descending half-cycle; his lifespan is given as 8,400,000 pūrvas

realization_account.text: After renouncing kingship he undertook a long fast; he attained omniscience (kevala-jñāna) under a banyan tree and preached in the first samavasaraṇa of this era; his mother Marudevī, seeing his glory, became the first soul of this era to reach liberation (Śvetāmbara account).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The Śvetāmbara account makes Marudevī the first liberated soul of this era; Digambara accounts differ on her.

name: Ajitanātha
summary: The second Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the elephant. Parents: King Jitaśatru and Queen Vijayā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His cousin Sagara was the second world-emperor (cakravartin).

tradition.text: the second of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Sambhavanātha
summary: The third Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the horse. Parents: Jitāri and Senā. Born at Śrāvastī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the third of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Abhinandananātha
summary: The fourth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the monkey. Parents: Saṃvara and Siddhārthā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fourth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Sumatinātha
summary: The fifth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the curlew (krauñca) in Śvetāmbara lists; the ruddy goose (cakravāka) in Digambara lists. Parents: Megharatha (Megha) and Maṅgalā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fifth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

tradition.text: the sixth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

tradition.text: the seventh of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

tradition.text: the eighth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

name: Suvidhinātha (Puṣpadanta)
summary: The ninth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the makara (crocodile / sea-monster). Parents: Sugrīva and Rāmā. Born at Kākandī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His body is described as white. Not to be confused with the Digambara author Puṣpadanta (tch:puspadanta-acarya).

tradition.text: the ninth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

name: Śītalanātha
summary: The tenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the śrīvatsa mark in Śvetāmbara lists (a wish-fulfilling tree in some Digambara lists; low confidence). Parents: Dṛḍharatha and Nandā. Born at Bhadrilapura (Bhaddilapura); attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the tenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

name: Śreyāṃsanātha
summary: The eleventh Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the rhinoceros. Parents: Viṣṇu and Viṣṇu(-śrī) (low confidence). Born at Siṃhapurī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. The first vāsudeva, Tripṛṣṭha, lived in his time.

tradition.text: the eleventh of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Vāsupūjya
summary: The twelfth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the buffalo. Parents: Vasupūjya and Jayā. Born at Campā; attained nirvāṇa at Campā. The only Tīrthaṅkara to attain nirvāṇa at Campā; his body is described as red; Śvetāmbara accounts say he did not marry or rule.

tradition.text: the twelfth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Vimalanātha
summary: The thirteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the boar. Parents: Kṛtavarman and Śyāmā. Born at Kāmpilya; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. The Tamil Mērumantara Purāṇam makes Meru and Mandara his gaṇadharas.

tradition.text: the thirteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Anantanātha
summary: The fourteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the falcon (śyena) in Śvetāmbara lists; the porcupine in Digambara lists. Parents: Siṃhasena and Suyaśā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fourteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Dharmanātha
summary: The fifteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the thunderbolt (vajra). Parents: Bhānu and Suvratā. Born at Ratnapurī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fifteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Śāntinātha
summary: The sixteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the deer (antelope). Parents: Viśvasena and Acirā. Born at Hastināpura; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. He was also the fifth world-emperor (cakravartin) before renouncing; in a previous life as King Megharatha he offered his own flesh to save a pigeon from a hawk. He is invoked for peace (śānti) and widely worshipped.

tradition.text: the sixteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Kunthunātha
summary: The seventeenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the goat. Parents: Sūra (Sūrasena) and Śrī. Born at Hastināpura; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. He was also the sixth world-emperor.

tradition.text: the seventeenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Aranātha
summary: The eighteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the nandyāvarta diagram in Śvetāmbara lists; the fish in Digambara lists. Parents: Sudarśana and Devī (Mitrā). Born at Hastināpura; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. He was also the seventh world-emperor.

tradition.text: the eighteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Mallinātha (Mallī)
summary: The nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, emblem the water-jar (kalaśa), born at Mithilā to King Kumbha and Queen Prabhāvatī, attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. In the Śvetāmbara account (Jñātādharmakathā 1.8) Mallī was a princess who, courted by six kings (her companions in a former life), showed them a hollow golden image of herself filled daily with food that rotted within, to teach the impurity of the body, and then renounced with them; a woman Tīrthaṅkara is counted among the ten 'wonders' (accheras) of this era. In the Digambara account Mallinātha was a man.

tradition.text: the nineteenth Jina of this era

realization_account.text: Śvetāmbara: Mallī attained omniscience on the very day of her renunciation; her female birth resulted from a slight deceit in her past life as King Mahābala, who secretly undertook more fasts than his companions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: gender set to 'unknown' because the traditions disagree: female (Śvetāmbara, Yāpanīya-compatible), male (Digambara).

name: Munisuvrata
summary: The twentieth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the tortoise. Parents: Sumitra and Padmāvatī. Born at Rājagṛha; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His body is described as dark; Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Rāvaṇa lived in his era.

tradition.text: the twentieth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Naminātha
summary: The twenty-first Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the blue lotus (nīlotpala). Parents: Vijaya and Vaprā. Born at Mithilā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. Not to be confused with the royal sage Nami of Uttarādhyayana 9.

tradition.text: the twenty-first of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Neminātha (Ariṣṭanemi)
summary: The twenty-second Tīrthaṅkara, emblem the conch, son of Samudravijaya and Śivā of the Yādava (Hari) clan, born at Śauryapura, cousin of Kṛṣṇa. On the way to his wedding with Rājīmatī he heard the cries of animals penned for the feast, freed them and renounced; Rājīmatī too became a nun and steadied his brother Rathanemi in his vows (Uttarādhyayana 22). He attained omniscience and nirvāṇa on Mount Girnār (Ujjayanta / Raivataka). His body is described as dark.

tradition.text: the twenty-second Jina, preceding Pārśva by 84,000 years in the traditional chronology

realization_account.text: He renounced on seeing the animals to be killed for his own wedding feast and attained omniscience on Girnār.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Some scholars have argued for a historical core to Nemi; most treat him as legendary.

name: Pārśva (Pārśvanātha)
summary: The twenty-third Tīrthaṅkara, emblem the serpent, son of King Aśvasena and Queen Vāmā of Vārāṇasī. As a prince he rescued a pair of serpents burning in the fire of the ascetic Kamaṭha; reborn as Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī, they later shielded him with their hoods when Kamaṭha, reborn as the god Meghamālin, assailed his meditation with storm and flood. He taught the fourfold restraint (cāujjāma: non-violence, truth, not stealing, non-possession) and his followers wore garments; he lived a hundred years and attained nirvāṇa on Sammeda Śikhara (Pārasnāth hill). Mahāvīra's parents were followers of his teaching, and his followers (such as Keśin) joined Mahāvīra's community.

tradition.text: nirvāṇa 250 years before Mahāvīra's (traditionally 777 BCE)

scholarly.text: probably historical; c. 9th–7th c. BCE (estimates vary)

realization_account.text: He attained omniscience after 84 days of ascetic practice, following Meghamālin's attack from which Dharaṇendra shielded him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Historicity 'historical' reflects the common scholarly view that Pārśva was a real teacher; the dates are uncertain.

name: Mahāvīra (Vardhamāna)
summary: The twenty-fourth and last Tīrthaṅkara of this era, emblem the lion. Born Vardhamāna to Siddhārtha of the Jñātṛ (Nāya) clan and Triśalā at Kuṇḍagrāma near Vaiśālī; renounced at thirty; for twelve and a half years practised severe austerities in silence, enduring hardships and attacks (Ācārāṅga 1.9); attained omniscience; taught for thirty years, founding the fourfold community with eleven gaṇadharas headed by Indrabhūti Gautama; attained nirvāṇa at Pāvā aged seventy-two. Śvetāmbaras add that his embryo was transferred from the brāhmaṇī Devānandā to Triśalā, that his mother saw fourteen dreams (sixteen for Digambaras), and that he married Yaśodā and had a daughter, Priyadarśanā; Digambaras deny the transfer and the marriage. Known in the Pali canon as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.

tradition.text: 599–527 BCE (the commonly used traditional reckoning: nirvāṇa 470 years before the Vikrama era; some Digambara reckonings differ)

scholarly.text: 6th–5th c. BCE; the nirvāṇa is variously dated by scholars between c. 527 and c. 425 BCE

realization_account.text: In the thirteenth year of his ascetic life, on the tenth of the bright half of Vaiśākha, outside Jṛmbhikagrāma on the bank of the Ṛjupālikā, under a śāla tree, squatting in the milking posture in the heat of the sun after a two-and-a-half-day fast without water, in deep (pure) meditation, he attained the infinite, supreme, unobstructed, complete and full knowledge and perception called kevala; at Pāvā, in his seventy-second year, he passed to nirvāṇa, freed from all suffering.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bāhubali (Gommaṭeśvara)
summary: Son of Ṛṣabha, who defeated his elder brother Bharata in single combat for the kingdom, then renounced in the moment of victory and stood motionless in meditation (kāyotsarga) for a year until creepers grew over him. Śvetāmbaras say his omniscience was delayed by pride until his sisters Brāhmī and Sundarī told him to 'get down from the elephant'; Digambaras say a lingering thought that he stood on Bharata's land delayed it. For Digambaras the first of this era to attain liberation. His 58-foot image (981 CE) at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa is anointed in the twelve-yearly Mahāmastakābhiṣeka.

realization_account.text: He stood a full year in body-abandonment; when the last obstacle (pride, or the thought of his brother's land) fell away he attained omniscience.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bharata (the first world-emperor)
summary: Eldest son of Ṛṣabha and first of the twelve world-emperors (cakravartin) of this era, after whom Bhāratavarṣa is named in Jain tradition. He conquered the six divisions of Bharata-kṣetra; Digambaras (Ādipurāṇa) say he created the brāhmaṇas from among the laity who avoided trampling sprouts; Śvetāmbaras tell that he attained omniscience while looking in a mirror in his palace, seeing the body's unreality when a ring fell from his finger.

name: Marudevī
summary: Mother of Ṛṣabha; in the Śvetāmbara account the first soul of this era to attain liberation, reaching omniscience and nirvāṇa on elephant-back as she saw her son's samavasaraṇa.

name: Brāhmī
summary: Daughter of Ṛṣabha, to whom he taught writing — the Brāhmī script is named after her; she became a nun and head of the nuns in his community.

name: Sundarī
summary: Daughter of Ṛṣabha, to whom he taught arithmetic; she became a nun (Śvetāmbara accounts tell of her long austerities before Bharata allowed her to renounce).

name: Puṇḍarīka
summary: The first gaṇadhara of Ṛṣabha, who (Śvetāmbara tradition) attained liberation on Mount Śatruñjaya, the holiest Śvetāmbara pilgrimage hill (Puṇḍarīkagiri).

name: Sīmandhara
summary: One of the twenty 'living' (viharamāna) Tīrthaṅkaras now teaching in the Mahāvideha region, where liberation is always possible. Digambaras hold that Kundakunda travelled to him to hear the teaching; he is also the focus of devotion in the Kanji Swami movement.

name: Rājīmatī (Rājul)
summary: The bride Neminātha left on his wedding day; she became a nun and, sheltering in a cave, recalled his brother Rathanemi to his vows (Uttarādhyayana 22; Daśavaikālika 2).

name: Rathanemi
summary: Brother of Neminātha, a monk who was tempted on seeing Rājīmatī and was brought back to his vows by her rebuke.

name: Śreṇika (Bimbisāra)
summary: King of Magadha at Rājagṛha, a hearer of Mahāvīra, who (because of his faith) will be the first Tīrthaṅkara, Padmanābha, of the next ascending half-cycle, though he first suffers in hell for past deeds.

name: Indrabhūti Gautama
summary: The first and chief gaṇadhara of Mahāvīra, a brāhmaṇa of Gobbara near Rājagṛha, who came to refute him and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his doubt whether a soul exists. The questioner of the Bhagavatī and the addressee of 'Gautama, be not careless for a moment' (Uttarādhyayana 10). His attachment to his teacher delayed his omniscience, which he attained on the night of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa (Śvetāmbara account) — remembered at Dīvālī; he is invoked for success and wealth ('Gautama-svāmī').

tradition.text: contemporary of Mahāvīra; liberated 12 years after him (Śvetāmbara)

realization_account.text: His love for Mahāvīra was the last bond; when he learned of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa he grieved, reflected on the Jina's detachment, and attained omniscience that night.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Agnibhūti
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether karma exists. Brother of Indrabhūti.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Vāyubhūti
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether the soul is other than the body. Brother of Indrabhūti.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Vyakta
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether the elements (and all things) are real or empty.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Sudharman
summary: The fifth gaṇadhara, whose doubt was whether beings are reborn in the same kind; the only gaṇadhara besides Gautama to survive Mahāvīra, he became head of the community, and the Śvetāmbara Aṅgas are his recension, addressed to his pupil Jambū ('I have heard, O long-lived one…'). All later Śvetāmbara monks trace their descent to him.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience twelve years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa and liberation eight years later (Śvetāmbara account; moderate confidence).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Maṇḍika (Maṇḍita)
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt concerned bondage and liberation.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Mauryaputra
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether gods exist.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Akampita
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether hell-beings exist.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Acalabhrātṛ
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether merit and demerit (puṇya, pāpa) exist.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Metārya
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether there is another world (rebirth).

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Prabhāsa
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether liberation (nirvāṇa) exists.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Candanā (Candanabālā)
summary: The first nun of Mahāvīra's community and head of its nuns (the Kalpa Sūtra gives 36,000 nuns under her). A princess of Campā sold into slavery, shackled and shaven by a jealous mistress, she fulfilled Mahāvīra's secret vow (abhigraha) by offering him boiled beans from a winnowing basket, ending his long fast; she later took initiation. Śvetāmbara stories tell that she attained omniscience after her pupil Mṛgāvatī did.
alt_names: Vasumatī (her birth name in some accounts)

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience when, asking forgiveness of her pupil Mṛgāvatī who had attained it first, she saw the humility of her disciple (Śvetāmbara account).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Jambū (Jambūsvāmin)
summary: Pupil of Sudharman and the last person of this era to attain omniscience in Bharata-kṣetra: a merchant's son who renounced on his wedding night with his eight brides (and converted the thief Prabhava who came to rob them). After him, the Śvetāmbaras say, certain things were lost — including the naked Jinakalpa mode, the highest knowledges and liberation in this region. The Aṅgas are addressed to him.

tradition.text: liberated 64 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa (Śvetāmbara); 62 years for the three omniscients (Digambara)

realization_account.text: The last omniscient (kevalin) of this era in Bharata-kṣetra.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Prabhava
summary: A thief who came to rob Jambū on his wedding night and was converted; Jambū's successor as head of the Śvetāmbara community.

name: Śayyambhava
summary: A brāhmaṇa converted by Prabhava's disciples; successor of Prabhava, who according to tradition composed the Daśavaikālika from the Pūrvas for his son Manaka, who had only six months to live.

name: Yaśobhadra
summary: Successor of Śayyambhava; teacher of both Sambhūtavijaya and Bhadrabāhu.

name: Sambhūtavijaya
summary: Elder who with Bhadrabāhu succeeded Yaśobhadra; teacher of Sthūlabhadra.

name: Bhadrabāhu (the śrutakevalin)
summary: The last 'scripture-omniscient' (śrutakevalin), who knew all fourteen Pūrvas. Śvetāmbaras say that during a twelve-year famine he withdrew to Nepal to practise the 'great breath' (mahāprāṇa) meditation and there taught the Pūrvas to Sthūlabhadra; they ascribe to him the Kalpa Sūtra, three Chedasūtras and the niryuktis. Digambaras say he foresaw the famine, led the saṅgha south to Karnataka with the Maurya emperor Candragupta as his disciple, and died by sallekhanā on Candragiri at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa; those who stayed in the north adopted clothes.

tradition.text: died 170 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa (Śvetāmbara) / 162 years (Digambara); contemporary of Candragupta Maurya

notes: Scholars distinguish a later Bhadrabāhu (II) to whom the niryuktis may belong.

name: Bhadrabāhu II
summary: A later Bhadrabāhu to whom some scholars (and a late Śvetāmbara tradition, which makes him brother of the astronomer Varāhamihira) assign the niryuktis; his identity and date (c. 5th–6th c. CE) are uncertain.

name: Sthūlabhadra
summary: Son of the Nanda minister Śakaṭāla, who lived twelve years with the courtesan Kośā, renounced, and later spent a rainy season in her house without falling (celebrated as the model of chastity). He presided over the council at Pāṭaliputra after the famine; he learned the fourteen Pūrvas from Bhadrabāhu, but after he displayed a magical power (turning into a lion before his sisters) Bhadrabāhu taught him the last four as text only, without their meaning — the beginning of the loss of the Pūrvas.

realization_account.text: Invoked in the auspicious verse 'maṅgalaṃ sthūlabhadrādyā' after Mahāvīra and Gautama (Śvetāmbara form).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mahāgiri
summary: Pupil of Sthūlabhadra who, the Śvetāmbaras say, tried to revive the Jinakalpa (naked, solitary) practice.

name: Suhastin
summary: Pupil of Sthūlabhadra who converted the Maurya king Samprati, grandson of Aśoka, a great patron of Jainism; the Kalpa Sūtra's list of gaṇas and kulas descends largely from his pupils.

name: Samprati
summary: Maurya king, grandson of Aśoka, converted by Suhastin, who (Śvetāmbara tradition) spread Jainism beyond Magadha and built many temples.

name: Candragupta Maurya
summary: Founder of the Maurya empire. Digambara tradition (and inscriptions at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa) says he renounced, followed Bhadrabāhu south and died by sallekhanā on Candragiri; Hemacandra's Śvetāmbara account also makes him end his life as a Jain.

name: Kālaka (Kālakācārya)
summary: Elder remembered in the Kālakācāryakathā: to free his sister, the nun Sarasvatī, abducted by King Gardabhilla of Ujjayinī, he brought the Śaka kings; he also moved the Paryuṣaṇa (Saṃvatsarī) from the fifth to the fourth of Bhādrapada at the request of King Sātavāhana, a date the Tapā Gaccha keeps.

tradition.text: c. 1st c. BCE

name: Āryarakṣita
summary: Elder credited with dividing the teaching into four anuyogas (conduct, narrative, calculation, substance) and with the Anuyogadvāra; the Trairāśika schism of Rohagupta and the Goṣṭhāmāhila schism are placed in his time.

tradition.text: c. 1st c. CE (tradition's chronology)

name: Vajrasvāmin
summary: The last to know ten Pūrvas (daśapūrvin) in the Śvetāmbara account; famous child-renouncer and wonder-worker who (the stories say) carried the saṅgha through a famine by magical power.

tradition.text: c. 1st c. CE

name: Śyāmārya (Ārya Śyāma)
summary: Elder credited with the Prajñāpanā, the fourth Upāṅga.

name: Skandila
summary: Presided over the council (vācanā) at Mathurā (c. 827–840 years after the nirvāṇa) that restored the canon after a famine; the 'Māthurī' recension.

tradition.text: c. 4th c. CE

name: Nāgārjuna (Jain elder of Valabhī)
summary: Presided over a council at Valabhī contemporary with Skandila's at Mathurā; variant readings of his 'Nāgārjunīya' recension are noted in the commentaries. Not the Buddhist Nāgārjuna.

tradition.text: c. 4th c. CE

name: Devarddhigaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa
summary: Presided over the council at Valabhī (980 or 993 years after the nirvāṇa, i.e. 453 or 466 CE) at which the Śvetāmbara canon was written down, reconciling the Māthurī and Vālabhī recensions; some identify him with Devavācaka, author of the Nandī.

tradition.text: 980 or 993 years after the nirvāṇa

name: Devavācaka
summary: Author of the Nandī Sūtra (c. 5th c. CE); sometimes identified with Devarddhigaṇi.

name: Vīrabhadra
summary: A monk of Mahāvīra's time to whom tradition ascribes several Prakīrṇakas (Catuḥśaraṇa, Bhaktaparijñā, and others).

name: Jamāli
summary: Nephew and (Śvetāmbara) son-in-law of Mahāvīra, husband of Priyadarśanā; the first schismatic (nihnava). Lying ill, he held that 'what is being done is not yet done' against Mahāvīra's 'what is being done is done' (Bhagavatī 9.33) and led away a group of monks; Priyadarśanā at first followed him and then returned.

name: Rohagupta (Ṣaḍulūka)
summary: The sixth schismatic in Śvetāmbara lists, who in debate asserted three categories — soul, non-soul and 'no-soul' (trairāśika) — and would not recant when refuted by his teacher Śrīgupta; the Jain tradition makes him the founder of the Vaiśeṣika system with its six categories.
notes: The identification with Vaiśeṣika is the Jain tradition's account (reported_by_opponent from the Vaiśeṣika point of view).

name: Śivabhūti (Sahasramalla)
summary: In the Śvetāmbara account the founder of the Boṭika (Digambara) schism at Rathavīrapura 609 years after the nirvāṇa: when his teacher Āryakṛṣṇa tore up a precious blanket the king had given him, he declared that the Jinakalpa nakedness was the true path and went naked; his sister Uttarā, told that women may not go naked, kept her clothes — hence the Boṭikas deny liberation to women.

realization_account.text: This is the Śvetāmbara (opponent's) account of the origin of the Digambaras; the Digambaras do not accept it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Keśin (Keśikumāra Śramaṇa)
summary: A monk of Pārśva's line who met Gautama at Śrāvastī and, after their dialogue on the four and five vows and on clothing, accepted Mahāvīra's teaching (Uttarādhyayana 23); in the Rājapraśnīya he converts King Paesi.

name: Paesi (Pradeśin)
summary: King of Śvetavikā who doubted the soul, tested it by experiments on condemned criminals, and was convinced by Keśin that the soul is distinct from the body (Rājapraśnīya); reborn as the god Sūryābha.
notes: Parallels King Pāyāsi of the Pali Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23).

name: Ārdraka (Ārdrakakumāra)
summary: A prince, in the tradition from a distant land, who became a monk of Mahāvīra and on his way to him debated Gośāla, Buddhists, brāhmaṇas, Vedāntin (ekadaṇḍin) ascetics and elephant-killing hermits (Sūtrakṛtāṅga 2.6).

name: Jayantī
summary: A laywoman of Kauśāmbī, sister-in-law of King Śatānīka, whose questions to Mahāvīra (on sleep and wakefulness, strength and weakness, and whether all beings capable of liberation will be liberated) are recorded in the Bhagavatī (12.2); she later became a nun.

name: Ānanda (lay disciple)
summary: A householder of Vāṇijagrāma, the first of the ten lay disciples of the Upāsakadaśā, who took the twelve lay vows and the eleven pratimās, gained clairvoyance (avadhi-jñāna) and died in peace; when Gautama doubted the extent of his clairvoyance, Mahāvīra sent Gautama to apologize to the layman.

name: Saddālaputra
summary: A potter of Polāsapura, formerly a lay follower of Gośāla, converted by Mahāvīra's argument about his pots (if effort were nothing, why punish a man who smashes them?) (Upāsakadaśā 7).

name: Gajasukumāla
summary: Younger brother of Kṛṣṇa who became a monk under Ariṣṭanemi; meditating in a cremation ground, he kept equanimity while the brāhmaṇa Somila placed burning coals in a clay rim on his head, and attained liberation that night (Antakṛddaśā).

name: Meghakumāra
summary: Son of King Śreṇika who became a monk; distressed by being jostled on his first night, he was reminded by Mahāvīra of his past life as an elephant who held up his foot for days to spare a hare (Jñātādharmakathā 1.1).

name: Kūṇika (Ajātaśatru)
summary: King of Magadha, son of Śreṇika, who visits Mahāvīra in state in the Aupapātika and wars against Ceṭaka of Vaiśālī in the Nirayāvalikā.

name: Kundakunda
summary: The most revered Digambara ācārya, author of the Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra, Niyamasāra, Pañcāstikāyasāra, the Aṣṭapāhuḍa and the Bārasa Aṇuvekkhā (tradition credits him with eighty-four pāhuḍas). He taught the pure self from the standpoint of ultimate reality (niścaya) and the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra) as its teaching device, and upheld monastic nudity against clothed renunciation. The Mūla Saṅgha calls itself his lineage (Kundakundānvaya); Tamil Jains identify him with Elācārya, to whom they ascribe the Tirukkuṟaḷ.

tradition.text: 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE (Digambara paṭṭāvalīs)

realization_account.text: He travelled by magical power to the living Tīrthaṅkara Sīmandhara in Videha and heard the teaching directly (Devasena's Darśanasāra; later Digambara legend).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Dharasena
summary: Digambara teacher at the Candra cave of Girinagar (Girnār) who knew part of the Pūrvas; fearing the loss of scripture he summoned two monks, tested them with defective spells which they corrected, and taught them the Karmaprābhṛta, which they set down as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama.

tradition.text: c. 683 years after the nirvāṇa

name: Puṣpadanta (ācārya)
summary: Pupil of Dharasena and co-author of the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, of which he wrote the opening (Satprarūpaṇā); the gods are said to have straightened his uneven teeth, hence the name.

name: Bhūtabali
summary: Pupil of Dharasena who completed the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, including its sixth part the Mahābandha; the bhūtas (spirits) are said to have worshipped him, hence the name.

name: Guṇadhara
summary: Author of the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa, held to have known part of the fifth Pūrva.

name: Yativṛṣabha
summary: Author of the cūrṇi-sūtras on the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa and (by tradition) of the Tiloyapaṇṇatti.

name: Vīrasena
summary: Digambara ācārya of the Pañcastūpa lineage who wrote the Dhavalā on the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama (816 CE) and began the Jayadhavalā; teacher of Jinasena.

name: Jinasena (author of the Ādipurāṇa)
summary: Pupil of Vīrasena, preceptor of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I; completed the Jayadhavalā (837 CE) and wrote the Ādipurāṇa, which defines Jain householder rites and the Jain brāhmaṇa; also the Pārśvābhyudaya.

name: Guṇabhadra
summary: Pupil of Jinasena who completed the Ādipurāṇa and wrote the Uttarapurāṇa and the didactic Ātmānuśāsana.

name: Jinasena of the Punnāṭa saṅgha
summary: Author of the Harivaṃśapurāṇa (783 CE); distinct from the author of the Ādipurāṇa.

name: Raviṣeṇa
summary: Author of the Sanskrit Padmapurāṇa (676–677 CE), the Digambara Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Amṛtacandra
summary: The great Digambara commentator on Kundakunda (Ātmakhyāti on the Samayasāra, Tattvapradīpikā on the Pravacanasāra, Samayavyākhyā on the Pañcāstikāya), author of the Samayasāra-kalaśa verses, the lay-conduct Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya and the Tattvārthasāra.

name: Jayasena (commentator on Kundakunda)
summary: Author of Tātparyavṛtti commentaries on Kundakunda's Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra and Pañcāstikāya, using a longer recension than Amṛtacandra's.

name: Padmaprabha Maladhārideva
summary: Commentator on the Niyamasāra (Tātparyavṛtti).

name: Vaṭṭakera
summary: Author of the Mūlācāra; some Digambaras identify him with Kundakunda.

name: Vasunandi
summary: Commentator on the Mūlācāra (Ācāravṛtti) and author of a Śrāvakācāra (c. 11th–12th c.).

name: Śivārya (Śivakoṭi)
summary: Author of the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā, who names his teachers and calls himself a 'hand-eater'; often placed by scholars in the Yāpanīya milieu.

name: Svāmi Kārttikeya (Svāmi Kumāra)
summary: Author of the Kārttikeyānuprekṣā on the twelve reflections; date and identity uncertain.

name: Nemicandra Siddhāntacakravartin
summary: Digambara master of the karma scriptures ('emperor of the siddhānta') who wrote the Gommaṭasāra, Labdhisāra and Trilokasāra for the minister Cāmuṇḍarāya.

name: Cāmuṇḍarāya
summary: Minister of the Western Gaṅga kings who erected the colossal image of Bāhubali (Gommaṭeśvara) at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa (c. 981 CE) and wrote the Kannada Cāmuṇḍarāya Purāṇa.

name: Indranandi
summary: Author of the Śrutāvatāra, the Digambara account of the descent and loss of scripture (c. 10th–12th c.; several Indranandis are known).

name: Devasena
summary: Author of the Darśanasāra (933 CE) on the origin of sects, and of the Ārādhanāsāra, Tattvasāra, Ālāpapaddhati and (attributed) Bhāvasaṃgraha.

name: Hariṣeṇa
summary: Author of the Bṛhatkathākośa (931–932 CE).

name: Ratnanandi (Ratnakīrti)
summary: Author of the 15th-c. Bhadrabāhucarita.

name: Prabhācandra (Digambara logician)
summary: 11th-c. Digambara logician of Dhārā, author of the Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa and Nyāyakumudacandra, which refute women's liberation and the omniscient's eating.

name: Somadeva
summary: Author of the Yaśastilaka (959 CE) and the political treatise Nītivākyāmṛta.

name: Vādībhasiṃha
summary: Author of the Kṣatracūḍāmaṇi and Gadyacintāmaṇi on Jīvandhara.

name: Puṣpadanta (Apabhraṃśa poet)
summary: 10th-c. Apabhraṃśa poet at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court of Mānyakheṭa, author of the Mahāpurāṇa, Jasaharacariu and Ṇāyakumāracariu.

name: Svayambhūdeva
summary: 9th-c. Apabhraṃśa poet, author of the Paumacariu and Riṭṭhaṇemicariu.

name: Sakalakīrti (Bhaṭṭāraka)
summary: 15th-c. Digambara bhaṭṭāraka of the Balātkāra gaṇa in Gujarat and Rajasthan, prolific author of Sanskrit purāṇas and caritras (Mahāvīrapurāṇa and others).

name: Ṭoḍarmal
summary: Paṇḍit of Jaipur (18th c.), leading lay scholar of the Digambara Terāpantha, author of the Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka and Hindi commentaries on the Gommaṭasāra.

name: Tāraṇa Svāmī
summary: Founder of the aniconic Tāraṇapantha in Bundelkhand (1448–1515), who taught the inner nature of the soul and veneration of scripture instead of images.

name: Ācārya Śāntisāgara
summary: Digambara monk (1872–1955) who revived the order of naked munis in northern India in the 20th c. and ended his life by sallekhanā; called 'cāritra-cakravartin'.

name: Ācārya Vidyāsāgara
summary: Digambara ācārya (1946–2024), initiator of a very large order of naked monks and of āryikās, poet in Hindi and Sanskrit (Mūkamāṭī).

name: Pampa (Ādikavi)
summary: 10th-c. Kannada poet, author of the Ādipurāṇa (941) and the Vikramārjunavijaya.

name: Śivakoṭyācārya (of the Vaḍḍārādhane)
summary: The traditional author of the Kannada Vaḍḍārādhane; authorship uncertain.

name: Śākaṭāyana (Pālyakīrti)
summary: Yāpanīya ācārya and grammarian at the court of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I, author of the Śabdānuśāsana with the Amoghavṛtti and of the Strīnirvāṇa- and Kevalibhukti-prakaraṇas.

name: Aparājitasūri
summary: Author of the Vijayodayā commentary on the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā, generally regarded as a Yāpanīya.

name: Śrīkalaśa
summary: Named by Devasena's Darśanasāra as the Śvetāmbara monk who founded the Yāpanīya saṅgha at Kalyāṇa (the Digambara polemical account; low confidence).

name: Jinabhadragaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa
summary: Śvetāmbara scholastic (6th–7th c.) whose Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya systematized the doctrines of knowledge, standpoints and the gaṇadharas' debates; also author of the Jītakalpa.

name: Saṅghadāsagaṇi
summary: Author of the Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya; a Saṅghadāsagaṇi is also author of the Vasudevahiṇḍī (whether the same person is uncertain).

name: Jinadāsagaṇi Mahattara
summary: 7th-c. author of cūrṇis on the Niśītha, Āvaśyaka, Nandī and other canonical texts.

name: Haribhadra
summary: Śvetāmbara ācārya (8th c.) — here in his role as commentator on the canon (Āvaśyaka, Daśavaikālika, Nandī, Anuyogadvāra), restorer of the Mahāniśītha, critic of the temple-dwelling monks, and author of the Lalitavistarā, which quotes the Yāpanīya-tantra on women's liberation.
notes: His yoga and philosophical works are covered by U35.

name: Śīlāṅka (Śīlācārya)
summary: 9th-c. Śvetāmbara commentator on the Ācārāṅga and Sūtrakṛtāṅga; a Śīlāṅka also wrote the Cauppannamahāpurisacariya (identity debated).

name: Abhayadevasūri
summary: Pupil of Jineśvara, the 'commentator on nine Aṅgas' (navāṅgī-vṛttikāra) in the 1060s.

name: Malayagiri
summary: 12th-c. Śvetāmbara commentator on many Upāṅgas, the Nandī, the Chedasūtras and the karma texts; contemporary of Hemacandra.

name: Vādivetāla Śāntisūri
summary: Early 11th-c. Śvetāmbara scholar and debater, author of the Śiṣyahitā commentary on the Uttarādhyayana.

name: Devendragaṇi (Nemicandra)
summary: Author of the Sukhabodhā commentary on the Uttarādhyayana (1073), with its Prakrit narratives.

name: Vimalasūri
summary: Author of the Prakrit Paumacariya, the earliest Jain Rāmāyaṇa; his sectarian affiliation is debated (some see Yāpanīya features).

name: Hemacandra
summary: Śvetāmbara polymath (1088/89–1172) at the Caulukya court of Siddharāja and Kumārapāla — here as author of the Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra and the Pariśiṣṭaparvan, the standard Śvetāmbara universal history and lives of the elders.
notes: His Yogaśāstra and philosophical works are covered by U35.

name: Vinayavijaya
summary: 17th-c. Tapā Gaccha monk, author of the Kalpasūtra-Subodhikā (1639) and the cosmological Lokaprakāśa; companion of Yaśovijaya.

name: Prabhācandrasūri (Śvetāmbara)
summary: Author of the Prabhāvakacarita (1277).

name: Jinaprabhasūri
summary: 14th-c. Kharatara monk at the court of Muhammad bin Tughluq, author of the Vividhatīrthakalpa and of ritual and hymn literature.

name: Jagaccandrasūri
summary: Founder of the Tapā Gaccha, named for his austerities (1228).

name: Devendrasūri (Tapā Gaccha)
summary: Pupil of Jagaccandra, author of the 'new' Karmagranthas on karma doctrine (13th c.).

name: Hīravijayasūri
summary: Tapā Gaccha leader (1527–1596) who visited Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri (1582) and obtained edicts restricting animal slaughter during Paryuṣaṇa.

name: Jineśvarasūri
summary: 11th-c. reformer who defeated the temple-dwelling monks in debate at the Caulukya court of Aṇahilapāṭaka (1024), winning the right of forest-dwelling (vasativāsī) monks to reside in the city; founder-figure of the Kharatara Gaccha.

name: Jinavallabhasūri
summary: Kharatara reformer (d. 1110) who continued the campaign against temple-dwelling monks.

name: Jinadattasūri
summary: Kharatara ācārya (1075–1154), the first 'Dādāguru', credited with converting many Rajput and other clans to Jainism.

name: Jinakuśalasūri
summary: Kharatara ācārya (1280–1332), one of the four Dādāgurus, venerated at dādābāḍī shrines.

name: Āryarakṣitasūri (founder of the Añcala Gaccha)
summary: 12th-c. founder of the Añcala (Vidhipakṣa) Gaccha; not the ancient Āryarakṣita.

name: Pārśvacandrasūri
summary: 16th-c. founder of the Pārśvacandra Gaccha, author of Gujarati glosses (ṭabo) on the Āgamas.

name: Rājendrasūri
summary: Mūrtipūjaka reformer (1827–1906), reviver of the Tristuti Gaccha and compiler of the Abhidhāna Rājendra, a Prakrit–Sanskrit encyclopedia of the canon.

name: Vijayānandasūri (Ātmārām)
summary: Punjabi Sthānakavāsī monk (1837–1896) who became a Mūrtipūjaka and revived the Śvetāmbara image-worshipping order in Punjab; he sent Virchand Gandhi to the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions.

name: Loṅkā Śāh
summary: Scribe of Ahmedabad (15th c.) who, copying the Āgamas, found no injunction to image worship or to the lax practices of the monks, and taught a return to the canon; source of the Loṅkā Gaccha and ultimately of the Sthānakavāsīs.

name: Lavjī Ṛṣi
summary: 17th-c. reformer from the Loṅkā yatis of Surat, one of the founders of the Sthānakavāsī order, associated with the constant wearing of the mouth-cloth.

name: Dharmasiṃha
summary: 17th-c. Sthānakavāsī founder-figure (Dariyāpurī sampradāya), author of vernacular glosses on the Āgamas.

name: Dharmadāsa
summary: 17th-c. Sthānakavāsī founder-figure whose twenty-two disciples are said to have headed the 'twenty-two groups' (bāīs ṭolā).

name: Ācārya Ātmārām (Sthānakavāsī)
summary: Punjabi Sthānakavāsī scholar (1882–1962), first ācārya of the united Śramaṇa Saṅgha (1952), translator and commentator of Āgamas.

name: Raghunāth (Sthānakavāsī ācārya)
summary: 18th-c. Sthānakavāsī ācārya in Marwar and the teacher from whom Bhikṣu separated in 1760.

name: Ācārya Bhikṣu (Bhīkhaṇjī)
summary: Founder (1726–1803) of the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth; he left the Sthānakavāsī order of Raghunāth in 1760 over monastic laxity and the definition of dharma, gave the order a single ācārya and a written code (maryādā), and wrote extensively in Rajasthani verse.

name: Jayācārya (Jītmal)
summary: Fourth ācārya of the Terāpanth (1803–1881), who organized its institutions, instituted the annual festival of the code (Maryādā Mahotsava) and wrote a Rajasthani verse rendering of the Bhagavatī.

name: Ācārya Tulsī
summary: Ninth ācārya of the Terāpanth (1914–1997), founder of the Aṇuvrata movement of 'small vows' for all people (1949), of the samaṇ/samaṇī order and of the Jain Vishva Bharati; directed the Lāḍnūn edition of the Āgamas.

name: Ācārya Mahāprajña (Muni Nathmal)
summary: Tenth ācārya of the Terāpanth (1920–2010), editor of the Āgamas, author on anekānta and non-violence, and creator of prekṣā-dhyāna meditation.

name: Ācārya Mahāśramaṇa
summary: Eleventh ācārya of the Terāpanth (b. 1962).

name: Tiruttakkatēvar
summary: Jain monk-poet, author of the Cīvakacintāmaṇi (c. 9th–10th c.); tradition makes him a Cōḻa prince.

name: Tōlāmoḻittēvar
summary: Jain poet, author of the Cūḷāmaṇi.

name: Muṉṟuṟai Araiyaṉār
summary: Jain poet, author of the Paḻamoḻi Nāṉūṟu.

name: Kaṇimētāviyār
summary: Jain poet, author of the Ēlāti and the Tiṇaimālai Nūṟṟaimpatu.

name: Kāriyācāṉ
summary: Jain poet, author of the Ciṟupañcamūlam.

name: Pavaṇanti
summary: Jain grammarian, author of the Naṉṉūl (c. 13th c.).

name: Amitacākarar
summary: Jain prosodist, author of the Yāpparuṅkalam and Yāpparuṅkalakkārikai (11th c.).

name: Vāmaṉa Muṉivar
summary: 14th-c. Tamil Jain monk, author of the Mērumantara Purāṇam and of the Samayadivākaram commentary on the Nīlakēci.

name: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ
summary: Traditional author of the Cilappatikāram, a Cēra prince turned ascetic; his Jain affiliation is contested.
